text: The Depression was responsible, first, for creating the mass electorate without which the Nazi Party would have remained marginal. Registered unemployment rose from about 1.4 million in 1928 to more than six million by early 1932, and the Nazi vote rose with it: from 2.6 per cent and twelve seats in May 1928, to 18.3 per cent and 107 seats in September 1930, to 37.3 per cent and 230 seats in July 1932, when the party became the largest in the Reichstag. The correlation is not itself the explanation; the mechanism was that the Depression destroyed the security of groups that had previously voted for the moderate and conservative parties. The agrarian crisis that had begun in 1928 ruined the Protestant farming north, so that Schleswig-Holstein gave the Nazis an absolute majority of 51 per cent in July 1932, and the small-business Mittelstand, threatened with ruin and frightened by a Communist vote that grew from 10.6 per cent in 1928 to 16.9 per cent in November 1932, turned to a party that promised national community and the destruction of Marxism. The Depression mattered because it gave the Nazi message an audience that had not existed in 1928. Economic collapse was therefore responsible for the Nazi Party's electoral rise to a degree no other factor matched.
